subject: English
passage: Lynda Mezdad and colleagues analyzed the dietary compositions of more than a hundred marine species from coral reef sites in the Caribbean spanning from 8,000 years ago to the present. They found that the species maintained genetically distinct feeding patterns characteristic of isolated Caribbean ecosystems until approximately 1,500 years ago, at which point there was substantial dietary overlap with Pacific marine species. Furthermore, beginning around 1,500 years ago, some sites contain shell fragments consistent with a Pacific origin, like abalone varieties, but the local communities show no evidence of having undertaken long-distance ocean voyages. From this, Mezdad and colleagues concluded that around 1,500 years ago ______
prompt: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people from the Caribbean began to reach the Pacific, where they acquired marine species and shell fragments such as abalone varieties.
choices.B: abalone shells and other Pacific materials began to be exchanged for marine species from the Caribbean.
choices.C: marine species and shell fragments like abalone varieties began to be transported from the Pacific to the Caribbean.
choices.D: marine species from the Pacific began to be exchanged for abalone shells and other materials from the Caribbean.

explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it presents the conclusion that most logically follows from the text's discussion of Mezdad and colleagues' findings about Caribbean reef sites. The text states that dietary analysis of many marine species from Caribbean sites dating from the last 8,000 years revealed that the species maintained genetically distinct feeding patterns (that is, they didn't share dietary characteristics with species from other regions) until about 1,500 years ago, when there is evidence that the species began showing dietary overlap with Pacific marine species. The text also indicates that around the same time, the sites began to contain abalone shells and other fragments seeming to be from the Pacific, even though there is no evidence that the local communities undertook long-distance ocean voyages. Because there is evidence of Pacific marine species influence and Pacific shell fragments at Caribbean sites beginning about 1,500 years ago but no evidence of the communities' long-distance travel around that time, it's reasonable to infer that Mezdad and colleagues concluded that marine species and shell fragments like abalone varieties were transported to the Caribbean from the Pacific, starting around 1,500 years ago.
